name: Inverse gambler's fallacy
statement: Someone who sees one improbable outcome concludes that the process must have run many times before, though earlier trials cannot change what this trial did.
meaning: The inference runs backwards, from an outcome to a history. A gambler walks into a casino, sees a double six on the nearest table, and decides the shooter must have been at it for a while. The rolls are independent, so the number that came before does not alter the chance that the roll on view was a double six. What a long run of rolls does raise is the chance that a double six came up somewhere in it, and Hacking's charge is that the two are being run together. Two things separate this from the gambler's fallacy. That one predicts the next outcome from the run just seen; this one reconstructs an unseen past from a single outcome. And what it infers is how many trials there were, not how they came out.

origin.note: The paper is "The inverse gambler's fallacy: the argument from design. The anthropic principle applied to Wheeler universes", Mind 96(383), 331-340. Its target was cosmological rather than psychological. Goff records that Hacking aimed the charge at John Wheeler's oscillating-universe theory, in which universes succeed one another in time. The Stanford Encyclopedia's fine-tuning entry states that Hacking counted only those versions of the argument guilty which infer a temporal sequence of universes. Roger White extended the charge to multiverses of every kind in 2000. The Mind paper could not be obtained for this entry, so both of those descriptions of it are read off Goff and the encyclopedia rather than off Hacking.

evidence: The fallacy was named by a philosopher and measured by psychologists twenty-two years later. Oppenheimer and Monin ran three studies. In Study 1, 108 Stanford undergraduates imagined walking into a room where a man was flipping a coin five times. Told that all five came up heads, they put the number of flips before they entered at a mean of 16.2; told of three heads and two tails, at 8.7. That gap gave t(106) = 2.17, p < .05, d = .42, after one outlier was dropped. Study 2a moved the scene to a casino and used 80 undergraduates. Three dice all showing six drew a mean estimate of 34.2 earlier rolls, two dice both showing six drew 10.6, and three dice showing two sixes and a three drew 3.2. The omnibus test was F(2, 77) = 4.8, p < .05, with pairwise ds of .56, .67 and .69. Study 2b put two of those outcomes to the same 31 people; 28 gave usable numbers, the means were 20.4 and 12.7, and a paired test on log-transformed data gave t(27) = 2.67, p < .05, d = .88. Half of that sample gave the same answer to both. Study 3 carried the design into everyday stories, from a lottery ticket to a dog bite. Sixteen were written and 15 analysed, 31 Princeton participants took part and 30 entered the model, which fitted 435 usable answers. The rare version of a story drew larger estimates of how often the protagonist had done the thing before, b = 0.74, SE 0.27, t = 2.73, p = .006 by Markov chain Monte Carlo. Rated unlikelihood accounted for the gap: with the likelihood rating in the model, the rare against common contrast fell to t = 0.58, p = .54. The casino scenario is close to the case Hacking argued from, a gambler who sees a double six and asks how long the dice have been rolling.

replication.headline: The dice scenario went to 36 samples and 5,942 people in Many Labs 1 and came back at about six-tenths of a standard deviation, a little under the original estimate.
replication.detail: Many Labs 1 ran Oppenheimer and Monin's Study 2a as one of its 16 effects, dropping the two-dice condition and keeping the contrast between three sixes and two sixes with a three. Across 36 samples and 5,942 participants the unweighted estimate was d = 0.59, 99% CI 0.49 to 0.70, against the original d = 0.69, 95% CI 0.16 to 1.21 as Klein and colleagues report it. The weighted estimate was 0.61, 99% CI 0.54 to 0.68, the median across samples 0.61, and the aggregate test t = 24.01 on 5,940 degrees of freedom, p < .001. The effect came out positive and significant at 83% of the samples and non-significant at the other 17%; no sample ran the other way. Heterogeneity was Q = 50.83 on 35 degrees of freedom, p = .04, with I-squared of 0.229, and the paper's two moderator tests, United States against international samples and laboratory against online, returned p = .53 and p = .56. Matthews then tested the version Oppenheimer and Monin had said was untested, asking 207 people to judge the outcome immediately before a streak of four rather than the length of the run. For coin flips the preceding outcome was judged likely to have been the opposite one, t(50) = -3.98 looking backwards and t(52) = -3.85 looking forwards, both p < .001, and the backward and forward judgements did not differ. For basketball shots neither direction showed any bias.

study.cite: Klein, R. A., Ratliff, K. A., Vianello, M., et al. (2014). Investigating variation in replicability: A "Many Labs" replication project. Social Psychology, 45(3), 142-152.

limits: What has been measured is a weaker claim than the one Hacking attacked, and Oppenheimer and Monin say so on their second page. Hacking and White argue that the fallacy lies in inferring that prior trials exist at all. The studies instead hand the participant a process already running and ask only how long it has run. No study of the inference to the existence of unobserved trials was located. A PubMed search for the phrase returns three records, the only one of them on this subject being Goff's philosophy paper in Synthese, and Crossref, Semantic Scholar and general web search produced philosophical argument rather than experiments. No meta-analysis of the effect was located in those same searches. Matthews raises a second reading of the estimates: a participant may be answering how many trials would be needed while waiting for such an outcome, which is a sound inference and does give a longer answer for rarer outcomes. Oppenheimer and Monin anticipate that reading, note that their scenario specifies an arbitrary moment of arrival, and treat it in two footnotes; Matthews's own task is not open to it. Their Study 3 numbers are heavily skewed, which is why the analysis is on a log scale: the mean estimate for a lottery winner's earlier tickets is 78,287, its 20% trimmed mean 857.89 and its median 150. Four of the papers behind the philosophical half of this entry could not be obtained. Hacking (1987), Leslie (1988) and McGrath (1988) sit behind Oxford Academic, and White (2000) behind Wiley; PhilPapers and JSTOR both refused automated access. What they argue is taken from Goff (2024), Landsman (2016) and the Stanford Encyclopedia's fine-tuning entry, all three read in full, and no figure or quotation is attributed to the four directly.
misreadings: The name is not a verdict on cosmology. Whether the inference from a fine-tuned universe to a multiverse commits the fallacy has been argued since 1988 and is open. The Stanford Encyclopedia lists McGrath, Leslie, Bostrom, Manson and Thrush, Juhl, Bradley, Epstein, Isaacs with Hawthorne and Russell, Saad and Ruyant as defending the inference, against Hacking, White, Draper and colleagues, and Landsman on the other side. Goff argues that the charge stands for the eternal-inflation multiverse in particular. Friederich argues that the question may have no determinate answer under established standards of rationality. The second error is treating every inference from a rare event to many trials as fallacious. Where the trial on view was selected because it was remarkable, many earlier trials are the right conclusion. McGrath's sleeper, woken only when someone rolls a double six, reasons correctly that several people were rolling, and so does Goff's Jane when told the doctor rolled repeatedly until a double six came up. The fallacy needs the observed trial to have been arbitrary. The third is treating the measured effect as the gambler's fallacy run backwards. Matthews argues that the gambler's fallacy is a judgement about which outcome comes next, and that Oppenheimer and Monin measured estimates of sequence length instead. His proposal is to call their finding retrospective representativeness and keep the older name for the direct analogue he tested. The fourth is confusing this with the hot hand, which reads a streak as evidence that the process is not random at all.
